newsitem.title: USA: G7 leaders push Clinton to keep troops in Bosnia.
newsitem.headline: G7 leaders push Clinton to keep troops in Bosnia.

text.p: European leaders expressed concern to U.S. President Bill Clinton at a Group of Seven summit on Friday night about U.S. plans to withdraw troops from a NATO peacekeeping force in Bosnia next year but Clinton stuck to his position.

The G7 leaders plus Russian President Boris Yeltsin began their three-day summit in the shadow of the Rocky Mountains with a working dinner before formal sessions on political and economic issues on Saturday.
Ways to prevent a new cycle of bloodshed in Bosnia figured prominently over the lobster soup and roasted lamb.
Officials said the leaders also agreed to send French and Japanese envoys to assess the situation in Cambodia, where the government had just announced the capture of Khmer Rouge strongman Pol Pol.
Clinton aide Dan Tarullo told reporters that "a number of leaders expressed concern about the stated U.S. date for withdrawal of U.S. troops from Bosnia next year."
U.S. troops number 8,500 out of the 31,000-strong NATO force policing a fragile peace in Bosnia. It is scheduled to withdraw in June 1998.
Diplomats have struggled to enforce political elements of the 1995 Dayton Peace Accords that separated Bosnia's former warring factions.
Nationalist authorities are complicating the situation by obstructing the return of refugees to conquered territory, and cooperation with war crimes inquiries is seen as behind schedule.
A source close to the French delegation said President Jacques Chirac made clear to Clinton that the Europeans did not want to see unilateral withdrawal of Americans from Bosnia.

"The military and civil aspects of the Dayton accords being partially achieved, the unilateral withdrawal of the Americans would create a problem for the Europeans," the source said, adding that Britain agreed with the French position.

Clinton, under pressure at home to bring back U.S. troops, told his partners they were taking the "wrong focus, that rather than thinking about when troops would be leaving, it was more important the leaders be thinking about how to make the civilian peace process work in Bosnia," Tarullo said.

The leaders discussed assigning responsibilities to the countries involved in Bosnia peacekeeping to make the Dayton accords work, such as strengthening local police, promoting elections and resettling refugees.
The G7 leaders -- of Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States -- and Yeltsin are expected to issue a statement on Bosnia before ending the "Summit of the Eight" on Sunday.

Protocol glitches infected the start of the dinner event at a 55-room Georgian mansion when Clinton was not on hand promptly to welcome Hashimoto, and German Chancellor Helmut Kohl's bus could not negotiate the winding driveway.

After the dinner the leaders abandoned protocol and departed en masse with no waiting limousines in sight. Kohl decided not to wait and strode off into the dark to find his bus. A couple of others followed.

Yeltsin, for his part, burst into Denver back on his old energetic form after missing last year's summit in France because of heart surgery. He blew kisses to cheering admirers and plunged unexpectedly into a crowd to meet local people.
"Denver is good," he said.

He ran into opposition in his drive to have Russia embraced as the eighth member of the G7 club. Clinton, sensitive to Russian concerns about NATO expansion, said Russia was "fully included" in the summit and at one point in a picture-taking session with Yeltsin referred to a "Group of Eight".
But France said there was a consensus among G7 nations that Russia should not be included in discussions of global economic and financial matters. Japan voiced disapproval as well.
The G7 leaders meet Saturday for an hour-long discussion of economic matters, the only summit event to which Yeltsin was not invited.
